name: Lao
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 12 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Enfield, N. J. 2004. Nominal classification in Lao: a sketch. Sprachtypologie und Universalienforschung (STUF) 57(2/3): 117-143. [MPG PuRe open postprint: scan of the published pages]
catalog_locator: p. 129, section 3, the two paragraphs between example (38) and examples (39)-(41)
catalog_quote: An important consequence of this difference in head-modifier ordering for numeral classifier versus modifier classifier contexts concerns stress patterns of Lao words. Non-monosyllabic Lao words and phrases are stress-final, resulting in pre-final elements becoming reduced. Many monomorphemic lexical items, for example, have sesquisyllabic (one-and-a-half-syllable) structure, in which a primary syllable (i.e. with full stress and with expression of the full range of contrasts in vowel length and lexical tone) is preceded by a reduced "half syllable" (with highly restricted phonotactic possibilities, and no contrast in vowel length or tone). For example, the word kabùang4 'ceramic tile' features a pre-syllable ka- (unstressed, without contrastive tone or vowel length) and a primary syllable -bùang4 (stressed, with long complex vowel and contrastive lexical tone). (This word contrasts with, for example, bùang4 'side' and kabong4 'caterpillar'.) This pattern also applies to polymorphemic words or phrases, and this stress-final word/phrase structure affects the phonological realization of certain morphemes taking different roles as grammatical components in phrasal combinations. An illustrative example concerns the classifier for non-human animates, which surfaces as too3 when in a numeral classifier position ... but as unstressed to0 when in a modifier classifier position ...
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lao is a lexical-tone language; in any word (or phrase) of more than one syllable, stress falls on the final syllable. Pre-final syllables are reduced: in sesquisyllabic words the initial minor syllable is unstressed, atonal and without length contrast, while the final full syllable carries stress, full vowel-length contrast and lexical tone (e.g. ka-'buang4 'ceramic tile'). The same right-edge prominence holds in polymorphemic words and phrases, so grammatical morphemes in non-final dependent position (modifier classifiers, class terms, deverbal prepositions) surface de-stressed and toneless.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No rule given. Enfield marks both primary and secondary stress in examples (39)-(41) (numeral-classifier vs modifier-classifier phrases) but does not state where secondary stress falls; full (non-reduced) non-final syllables evidently keep tone and some prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions to final stress. Related facts: a classifier is full-toned and stressed (too3) when phrase-final after a numeral but reduced (to0) when a modifier follows; paa3 'fish' reduces to atonal pa0 as a class-term prefix; in Type A reduplication (Enfield 2004 'Adjectives in Lao' sec. 4.2) the first copy is unstressed/atonal and the second fully stressed; deverbal prepositions and inner directionals are de-stressed and atonal (Enfield 2008: 158).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated explicitly for 'words and phrases' — right-edge stress of the phonological word/phrase, illustrated with monomorphemic sesquisyllables (word level) and classifier phrases (phrase level). Impressionistic, by the language's principal grammarian; not an instrumental study. The statement occurs inside a morphosyntax paper, not a dedicated phonology section; Enfield 2007 A Grammar of Lao (not accessible here) is expected to carry the canonical version.
new_statements.identity_note: Enfield's descriptions are of standard (Vientiane-based) Lao, 'Southwestern Tai, Laos/Thailand/Cambodia' — language-level laoo1244; no separate dialect glottocode needed. Isan (nort2741 'Northeastern Thai') is treated by Enfield as a variety but is not the object of the statement.

tone_statements.citation: Pornpottanamas, Warunsiri. 2023. Classifying "Lao" Ethnic Languages Spoken in Central Thailand Using Tonal Criteria: A Case Study of "Chachoengsao Lao". MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities 26(1): 1-24. doi:10.1163/26659077-25010024
tone_statements.quote: ... converted Vientiane Lao from the original three-tone system to a five-tone system with restricted distribution on checked syllables. ... According to Osatananda (2016), Tone 1 (T1) in Vientiane Lao, referred to as A123, is Low-Rising /24/. Tone 2 (T2) is referred to as A4 and DS123 or A4=DS123 is Mid-Rising /35/. Tone 3 (T3), referred to as B1234 and DS4 (B1234=DS4), is Mid Level /33/ whereas Tone 4 (T4), referred to as C1 and DL123 (C1=DL123), is Mid-Falling /31/. Tone 5 (T5), described as C234 and DL4 (C234=DL4), is High-Falling /42/.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.1 'Tone Box' (paragraph following Figure 1), article pp. 1-24
tone_statements.summary: Vientiane Lao has five tones: low-rising 24, mid-rising 35, mid level 33, mid-falling 31, high-falling 42 (after Osatananda 2016), from an older three-tone system; fewer tones on checked syllables.

tone_statements.citation: 益子幸江・鈴木玲子 [Masuko, Yukie & Suzuki, Reiko]. 2019. ラオ語の3語文における声調についての音響音声学的研究 [Acoustic Phonetic Study on the Tones of Three-word-sentence in Lao]. 東京外国語大学論集 (Area and Culture Studies) 99: 92-113. doi:10.15026/94295
tone_statements.quote: All possible combinations of Lao five tones assigned to each word, 125 patterns in total, were recorded. We measured F0 of three points in each pitch curve; the beginning, middle, and final points for level tones, and the beginning, either peak or bottom, and final points for falling or rising contour tones. The pitch curves of these patterns shows that tonal phonemic contrasts are shown by two marked characteristics, one is to reach the ‘bottom pitch’, the other, to reach ‘high’ of the speaker’s voice.
tone_statements.locator: p. 93, English Abstract; tone shapes from Fig. 1 (図1, quoted from Masuko & Suzuki 2017 Table 4), p. 95; near-level vs moving tones sec. 4.4, p. 97; shape grouping restated in sec. 6, p. 112
tone_statements.summary: Acoustic F0 study presupposing Lao's five tones: falling/convex group (1-3) vs rising/concave group (4-5), split by reaching the pitch floor and by 'high'; some tones nearly level; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: 益子幸江・鈴木玲子 [Masuko, Yukie & Suzuki, Reiko]. 2017. ラオ語の声調についての音響音声学的研究 [Acoustic Phonetic Study on Lao Tones]. 東京外国語大学論集 (Area and Culture Studies, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies) 94: 19-36.
tone_statements.quote: This study attempts to examine the acoustic phonetic characteristics of Lao tones not to show that five tones contrast to one another on equal terms, but to show hierarchical contrast. ... we found two major types in pitch curves, fall-rise type and (rise-) fall type. The former comprises the forth and the fifth, and the latter, the first, the second and the third tones. Within each type, contrast between 'marked' and 'unmarked' can be effectively observed.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.note: English abstract read: acoustic study of the five Lao tones in monosyllables, two-word phrases (all 25 tone combinations) and disyllables; argues for a hierarchical rather than flat five-way contrast: a fall-rise type (tones 4, 5) vs a (rise-)fall type (tones 1, 2, 3), with marked/unmarked members inside each type and context-dependent variants not reducible to coarticulation.

sources.note: Ch. IV 'Tone' (pp.9-12): Luang Prabang Lao is basically a monosyllabic tone language with a five-tone system, values on a 1-5 scale: (1) mid-falling /khàa/ [31], (2) falling /khâa/ [52], (3) mid-rising /kháa/ [34]~[45], (4) rising /khǎa/ [15] (near low-level [11] when a syllable follows without pause), (5) high falling-rising /khãa/ [534]; all five contrast in smooth (live) syllables, while checked syllables show only tone 2 vs 3 (long vowel/diphthong) and tone 1 vs 3 (short vowel), treated as conditioned allophones rather than separate tonemes; unlike Vientiane Lao there is no mid-level tone…

sources.note: Luang Phrabang Lao (Ban Xiang Man, Chom Phet, Luang Phrabang) has five tones on live syllables - Tone 1 High-Falling-to-Mid-Level /533/, Tone 2 Low-Rising /12/, Tone 3 Mid-Falling /32/, Tone 4 High Level-Falling /552/, Tone 5 Mid-Rising /34/, with DL/DS checked-syllable tones treated as allotones (Table 6, Gedney box); Lao Khrang of Ban Kut Chok (Chai Nat, Thailand) also five tones /515, 2131, 433, 552, 45/ (p.121, Table 5); compares both with Roffe 1956 and Brown 1965 five-tone analyses of LPL; semitone-normalised F0 plots; second half is a foreign-accent rating experiment with LPL judges.
